newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-RBA sees faster growth if inflation held.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-RBA sees faster growth if inflation held.

text.p: Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) governor Ian Macfarlane said on Thursday that the expansion in the economy will be longer than in the past if inflation is controlled.

In a speech to the Australia-Israel Chamber of Commerce in Melbourne, Macfarlane said he would not panic about a short period of unexpectedly strong growth but that Australia still had a lot further to go before supply side reforms have significantly lifted potential growth rates.
Macfarlane said that the bank does attract criticism from people who think that because it has an inflation target it means it is not interest in economic growth.
"...we are interested in sustaining a good inflation performance because we are interested in growth," he said.
"We say no-faster because post-war history has taught us that allowing inflation to rise actually harms growth propects in the longer term," the governor said.
The RBA aims to keep underlying inflation between two and three percent of the course of an economic cycle.

"This 'no faster' idea does not mean that we will panic at unexpectedly strong growth over a short period. It does mean we intend to avoid a "full steam ahead and damn the torpedoes" approach to policy," Macfarlane said.

The governor said claims that the central bank has a "speed limit" of 3.5 percent growth were not true although it would regard it as excessive if it was pushing up wages and prices in a way which would cause its medium-term target to be exceeded.
However, he said there are those who think a much higher figure for growth is achievable and should be pursued.

"Their approach would be to nominate a figure - I have seen five percent metioned - and expect the Reserve Bank to adjust monetary policy to achieve it in the long run (not just for one year)," Macfarlane said.

A growth rate of five percent is so far above Australia's historical performance Macfarlane said that unless specific improvements on the supply side of the economy have lifted the growth potential dramatically, it cannot be taken seriously.

"But even though there is some tentative evidence of higher productivity, I think we have still got a lot further to go before we could be confident that supply-side reforms have significantly lifted our potential growth rate," he added.
